chunks: How many wires UART needs. The question: How many wires does it have?
A basic two-way UART link needs three wires: transmit (TX), receive (RX), and ground. Each direction of data gets its own wire.
Ground is the shared reference that gives "high" and "low" their meaning. If data only flows one way, two wires are enough. Some links add two more wires for flow control.
Picture two towns joined by two one-way roads, one in each direction. Both roads can carry traffic at the same time, so neither side waits its turn.
Now picture a map that shows how high each road climbs. Both towns must measure height from the same sea level, or "uphill" means different things to each.
Ground is that shared sea level.
Three wires, the minimum for two-way UART. The moving dots show the direction each data wire carries.
The ground wire carries no data but defines what "high" and "low" mean for both receivers.
TX and RX: a device's transmit and receive pins. One device's TX goes to the other's RX. Ground (GND): the shared 0 volts reference both devices measure voltages from.
Full duplex: data moving in both directions at the same time. Separate wires make that possible. RTS and CTS: two optional wires that let a receiver tell the sender to pause.
This is called hardware flow control. Point-to-point: a link between exactly two devices, with no sharing.
Connect board A's TX to board B's RX. Connect B's TX to A's RX. Join the two grounds. That is three wires, and both boards can talk at once.
A GPS module that only streams data needs just its TX to the microcontroller's RX, plus ground, so two wires. Adding RTS and CTS makes five.
For comparison, SPI needs four wires plus one chip select for each extra device. That is the whole idea.
"The minimum for full duplex is three wires: TX, RX and a common ground. TX and RX are separate so each direction has its own wire.
Ground is the reference for the logic levels, so I always count it. If you only need data one way you can use two. Add RTS and CTS for hardware flow control and you're at five.
RS-485 variants use differential pairs instead, but it's the same framing.
Compared with SPI, which needs four plus a chip select per device, UART is very cheap in pins, but it's point-to-point."
